L7: ### Abstract
L8: Automated verification has become an essential part in the security evaluation of cryptographic protocols. Recently, there has been a considerable effort to lift the theory and tool support that existed for reachability properties to the more complex case of equivalence properties. In this paper we contribute both to the theory and practice of this verification problem.
L9: We establish new complexity results for static equivalence, trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity and provide a decision procedure for these equivalences in the case of a bounded number of sessions. Our procedure is the first to decide trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity exactly for a large variety of cryptographic primitives---those that can be represented by a subterm convergent destructor rewrite system. We implemented the procedure in a new tool, Deepsec.
L10: We showed through extensive experiments that it is significantly more efficient than other similar tools, while at the same time raises the scope of the protocols that can be analysed.

L42: ## Abstract
L43: We present an automatic iterative abstraction-refinement methodology in which the initial abstract model is generated by an automatic analysis of the control structures in the program to be verified. Abstract models may admit erroneous (or “spurious”) counterexamples. We devise new symbolic techniques which analyze such counterexamples and refine the abstract model correspondingly.
L44: The refinement algorithm keeps the size of the abstract state space small due to the use of abstraction functions which distinguish many degrees of abstraction for each program variable. We describe an implementation of our methodology in NuSMV. Practical experiments including a large Fujitsu IP core design with about 500 latches and 10000 lines of SMV code confirm the effectiveness of our approach.

L44@P1: Our paper follows the general framework established by Clarke, Grumberg, and
L45@P1: Long [10]. We assume that the reader has some familiarity with that framework. In
L46@P1: our methodology, atomic formulas are automatically extracted from the program that
L47@P1: describes the model. The atomic formulas are similar to the predicates used for abstraction by Graf and Saidi [13] and later in [11, 20]. However, instead of using the atomic
L48@P1: formulas to generate an abstract global transition system, we use them to construct an
L49@P1: explicit abstraction function. The abstraction function preserves logical relationships
L50@P1: among the atomic formulas instead of treating them as independent propositions. The
L51@P1: initial abstract model is constructed by adapting the existential abstraction techniques
L52@P1: proposed in [8, 10] to our framework. Then, a traditional model checker is used to determine whether

L59@P1: then the concrete model also satisfies the property. If the answer is no, then the model
L60@P1: checker generates a counterexample. Since the abstract model has more behaviors than
L61@P1: the concrete one, the abstract counterexample might not be valid. We say that such a
L62@P1: counterexample is spurious. Such abstraction techniques are also known as false negative techniques.
L63@P1: In our methodology, we provide a new symbolic algorithm to determine whether
L64@P1: an abstract counterexample is spurious. If the counterexample is not spurious, we report it to the user and stop. If the counterexample is spurious, the abstraction function
L65@P1: must be refined to eliminate it. In our methodology, we identify the shortest prefix of
L66@P1: the abstract counterexample that does not correspond to an actual trace in the concrete
L67@P1: model. The last abstract state in this prefix is split into less abstract states so that the
L68@P1: spurious counterexample is eliminated. Thus, a more refined abstraction function is obtained. Note that there may be many ways of splitting the abstract state; each determines
L69@P1: a different refinement of the abstraction function. It is desirable to obtain the coarsest
L70@P1: refinement which eliminates the counterexample because this corresponds to the smallest abstract model that is suitable for verification. We prove, however, that finding the
L71@P1: coarsest refinement is NP-hard. Because of this, we use a polynomial-time algorithm
L72@P1: which gives a suboptimal but sufficiently good refinement of the abstraction function.
